--- title: "The brain's response to a stimulus" --- The last page ended with an **event-related potential (ERP)**: the average of many epochs, showing what the brain does each time a stimulus appears. This page is about why averaging works, how to read the result, and how to compare two conditions. From here on we use the whole first visit, about 650 trials, already cleaned by the lab's pipeline in the way the last page described. ::: {#a62ac791 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import mne import eegtut epochs = mne.read_epochs(eegtut.epochs_file(visit=1)) print(len(epochs), "epochs,", len(epochs.ch_names), "channels") print("from", epochs.tmin, "to", epochs.tmax, "seconds around each stimulus") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 649 epochs, 64 channels from -0.19921875 to 0.80078125 seconds around each stimulus ``` ::: ::: The trial table from chapter 2 now travels with the epochs, one row per epoch: ::: {#ce7589d9 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} epochs.metadata.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
trial phase cat x y resp fb rt
0 0 train A 51.221880 67.957741 B Incorrect 913.4243
2 1 train B 53.235513 22.323357 A Incorrect 753.5773
4 2 train A 61.932367 74.086581 B Incorrect 902.2831
6 3 train B 68.833710 54.104766 A Incorrect 1523.7676
8 4 train B 82.982313 64.788213 B Correct 1687.6825
``` ::: ::: One housekeeping step. The pipeline marked one electrode as bad for this visit. We fill it in from its neighbours so that every plot has all 64 channels. ::: {#a08f3740 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("bad:", epochs.info["bads"]) epochs.interpolate_bads(); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` bad: ['PO7'] ``` ::: ::: ## Why we average Here is the signal at `PO8`, at the back of the head on the right, for a single trial, and then averaged over more and more trials. The dashed line is the moment the stimulus appeared. ::: {#35ccb062 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} eegtut.average_of_n(epochs, "PO8", counts=[1, 10, 100, 600]); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-erps_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=988 height=256} ::: ::: In one trial there is nothing to see. The brain's response to the stimulus is there, but it is a few microvolts, buried in ongoing activity several times larger that has nothing to do with the stimulus. That unrelated activity is different on every trial: up on one, down on the next. The response to the stimulus is nearly the same every time. So when trials are averaged, the unrelated activity cancels and the response remains. With 10 trials a shape begins to show; with 100 it is clear; with 600 the line before the stimulus is almost perfectly flat. ::: {.callout-note} ## The price of a clean average The noise shrinks with the *square root* of the number of trials. To halve the noise you need four times as many trials. This is why EEG experiments have hundreds of trials per condition, and why you should be wary of an ERP built from twenty. ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Try it Change `"PO8"` to `"Fz"` (front of the head). The response there has a different shape and is smaller. Does it take more trials before you can see it? ::: ## Reading an ERP The average over all epochs, at every electrode at once: ::: {#c85feeb6 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} erp = epochs.average() erp.plot_joint(); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-erps_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=778 height=414} ::: ::: Each line is one electrode; its colour shows where it is on the head (the small coloured head is the key). The maps along the top show the whole scalp at the moments marked by the grey lines. Read it as a sequence in time. - **Before 0** the lines are flat. Nothing has happened yet, and the baseline step set this stretch to zero. - **Just after 0.1 s** the first sharp peak appears, and the map shows it at the back of the head. This is visual cortex registering that something has appeared. It takes about a tenth of a second for the signal to travel from the eye to the cortex. - **From about 0.3 s** a slower, broader wave takes over, largest between 0.4 and 0.5 s over the back and middle of the head. This later activity is less about the eyes and more about what the participant does with the stimulus: recognising it, deciding, preparing a response. ERP peaks are named by direction and order or timing: **P1** is the first positive peak, **N1** the first negative one, **P3** (or P300) a large positive wave around 0.3 seconds or later. You will see these names in every ERP paper. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Positive and negative are not "more" and "less" A positive peak does not mean more brain activity than a negative one. The sign depends on which way the active patch of cortex happens to be facing and on the reference. What matters is when a peak occurs, where on the scalp, and how it changes between conditions. ::: ## Comparing two conditions An ERP on its own says "the brain responded". Experiments are about differences: does the response change with what was shown, or with what the participant did? The trial table lets us pick out any set of epochs by describing it. As an example, compare trials the participant got right with trials they got wrong: ::: {#b24185bc .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} correct = epochs["fb == 'Correct'"].average() wrong = epochs["fb == 'Incorrect'"].average() print(correct.nave, "correct trials,", wrong.nave, "wrong trials") mne.viz.plot_compare_evokeds({"correct": correct, "wrong": wrong}, picks="Pz"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 402 correct trials, 245 wrong trials ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-erps_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-2.png){width=779 height=587} ::: ::: The two lines have the same shape, and the one for correct trials runs a little higher for most of the epoch, by about one microvolt. Is that a real difference between getting it right and getting it wrong? Look at the stretch before time zero. Nothing can differ there, because the stimulus has not appeared yet, and still the orange line wobbles away from the blue one by more than half a microvolt. That wobble is what noise alone does to these averages, and the difference after the stimulus is not much bigger. So from this plot we cannot say. This is the habit to build: before believing a difference, ask how big a difference would turn up by chance. The stretch before the stimulus is a free look at the answer. A difference you can see in one participant is a reason to test it properly, not a result. Chapter 9 is about how to do that across participants. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Try it Compare the two categories instead: replace the two descriptions with `"cat == 'A'"` and `"cat == 'B'"`. The lines are much harder to tell apart. The brain must be treating A and B differently, since the participant can respond to them differently, but the difference is too subtle to see in an average at one electrode. Chapter 6 shows a more sensitive way to find it. ::: ## Summary - A single trial is mostly activity unrelated to the stimulus. Averaging many trials cancels it and leaves the response. - Noise falls with the square root of the number of trials. - Read an ERP by when its peaks occur and where they are on the scalp. Early peaks at the back of the head are visual; later, broader waves reflect what is done with the stimulus. - The sign of a peak is not the amount of activity. - Science is in the comparison between conditions, and a visible difference in one participant is where the work starts. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## In the lab's real pipeline ERPs are computed in the same way, per participant and per visit, and then compared across the five visits to ask how the response changes as the task is learned. The lab's scripts also build response-locked epochs, cut around the key press instead of the stimulus, which line up the activity leading to the response. :::
